questions.question_stem: A light client wants evidence that a particular transaction was included, what execution produced, and what world state resulted after a block. Which pairing best matches the lesson's block-root model?
questions.correct_answer: The transactions root commits to included inputs and ordering, the receipts root commits to execution outcomes, and the state root commits to the resulting world state.
incorrect_answers: The state root commits to included inputs and ordering, the transactions root commits to execution outcomes, and the receipts root commits to the resulting world state after execution.
The receipts root commits to inputs and ordering, the state root commits to execution outcomes, and the transactions root commits to the resulting world state.
The transactions root commits to the resulting world state, the receipts root commits to included inputs and ordering, and the state root commits to execution outcomes.
questions.explanation: Ethereum block headers use compact roots to commit to different claims. Transactions, receipts, and state are related, but each root answers a different verification question.

questions.question_stem: A student says, "The Merge must have restarted Ethereum because it replaced mining." Which response best reflects the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: The Merge replaced the consensus engine for block production and agreement, while existing contracts, balances, and application state continued.
incorrect_answers: The Merge replaced active contract balances and application state configurations, while the proof-of-work consensus engine remained entirely uninterrupted.
The Merge required all decentralized applications to manually redeploy on a brand new chain, while the execution layer and transaction history were deleted.
The Merge updated only client-side wallet software and user interface settings, while block production and consensus continued to rely on proof-of-work.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the Merge as a staged consensus-engine replacement. Ethereum's application state was not reset simply because proof-of-work mining ended.

questions.question_stem: Which comparison best captures how Ethereum's security cost changed from proof of work to proof of stake?
questions.correct_answer: Proof of work relied on continuous hashing expenditure, while proof of stake relies on bonded stake, signing duties, rewards, penalties, and slashable evidence.
incorrect_answers: Proof of work relied on validator security deposits, while proof of stake relies on ongoing hardware energy consumption and brute-force hashing calculations.
Proof of work relied on account age and coin distribution, while proof of stake removes validator rewards and ignores objective signing duties entirely.
Proof of work relied on choosing the chain with the largest block count, while proof of stake relies on selecting validators based on their individual net worth.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes a mechanism shift, not simply a label change. Ethereum moved from a hash-race security model to an economic model based on stake and protocol-enforced consequences.

questions.question_stem: In steady-state Ethereum PoS, why does a validator need more than just a signing key?
questions.correct_answer: The validator participates through execution and consensus clients while its validator process signs assigned proposal and attestation duties.
incorrect_answers: The validator participates through specialized GPU hashing hardware while its validator process signs blocks only after solving continuous puzzles.
The validator participates through web wallet interfaces while its validator process signs and decrypts the private keys of every active transacting user.
The validator participates through local memory pools while its validator process signs off-chain databases instead of active consensus protocols.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates execution, consensus, and signing responsibilities. Validators rarely propose blocks and frequently attest, but those duties depend on coordinated client software and assigned protocol roles.

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson emphasize randomized proposer and committee assignments?
questions.correct_answer: Randomization makes assignments harder to predict, target, or bias, supporting fair and resilient validator participation.
incorrect_answers: Randomization lets validators select any slot they prefer, eliminating the possibility of missed block proposal duties.
Randomization replaces checkpoint finality requirements, removing the need for validators to vote on epoch consensus.
Randomization guarantees that all active nodes have identical network latency, ensuring uniform client synchronization.
questions.explanation: Ethereum PoS needs a schedule, but a predictable or easily biased schedule would create attack opportunities. The lesson identifies RANDAO as Ethereum's production collective randomness mechanism, with VRFs and VDFs used only as comparisons or proposed enhancements.

questions.question_stem: A learner claims that every active Ethereum validator attests in every 12-second slot. What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: A committee attests in a given slot, and over an epoch the active validator set is scheduled so each active validator attests once.
incorrect_answers: Only the block proposer attests in a given slot, and over an epoch other validators wait until checkpoint finality is complete.
All validators attest in a given slot, and over an epoch their consensus votes are counted only if they also propose a new block.
Validators attest only when a fork occurs, and over an epoch ordinary slots are scheduled so they contain no active voting duties.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses slots and epochs to explain how validator work is scheduled. A slot has at most one proposal, while committee attestations are distributed across the epoch.

questions.question_stem: Two short-lived Ethereum PoS branches exist after a propagation delay. Branch A has more blocks, but Branch B has greater weight from validators' latest attestations. Under the lesson's fork-choice framing, which branch should honest nodes follow?
questions.correct_answer: Branch B, because LMD-GHOST follows the branch with the greatest latest stake-weighted attestation support from the last justified checkpoint.
incorrect_answers: Branch A, because Ethereum PoS implements the longest-chain rule exactly like proof of work and measures total computational hashing difficulty.
Whichever branch contains the oldest transaction, because early transaction timestamp ordering determines canonical history across all active nodes.
Neither branch, because any occurrence of a temporary fork permanently halts block production and requires a manual system reboot by validators.
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly rejects simple block-count reasoning for Ethereum PoS. LMD-GHOST resolves ordinary head disagreement using latest stake-weighted attestations.

questions.question_stem: Which statement best distinguishes LMD-GHOST, Casper-FFG, and Gasper in the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: LMD-GHOST chooses the current head, Casper-FFG justifies and finalizes epoch checkpoints, and Gasper combines those roles.
incorrect_answers: Casper-FFG chooses the current head, Gasper justifies and finalizes epoch checkpoints, and LMD-GHOST combines both roles.
Gasper chooses the current head, LMD-GHOST finalizes epoch checkpoints, and Casper-FFG combines those roles instead.
LMD-GHOST chooses transactions, Casper-FFG justifies and finalizes local validator databases, and Gasper combines those roles.
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against treating these names as interchangeable. Gasper combines fork choice and finality rather than replacing both with one undifferentiated mechanism.

questions.question_stem: A bridge is designing a settlement policy for high-value Ethereum deposits. Why does the lesson favor finalized checkpoints over simply waiting for a fixed number of blocks?
questions.correct_answer: Finalized checkpoints are economically hard to revert because reverting them implies at least one-third of stake must be slashable.
incorrect_answers: A fixed block count is completely irrelevant to security because pre-finality blocks contain no valid user transactions.
Finalized checkpoints are dynamically chosen each epoch because selecting them depends on the highest gas-price transactions recorded.
Waiting for more blocks is always functionally identical to finality because the Ethereum PoS consensus layer has no temporary forks.
questions.explanation: The lesson's settlement point is about the strength of the guarantee. Block production can continue amid short-term disagreement, but finality provides a much stronger economic commitment.

questions.question_stem: A validator signs two conflicting attestations that can both be shown on-chain. Why does this matter for the nothing-at-stake problem?
questions.correct_answer: Conflicting signatures create objective slashable evidence, so voting on incompatible histories can carry an economic penalty regardless of claimed intent.
incorrect_answers: Conflicting signatures are treated as harmless by the protocol, so validators are expected to vote on every potential fork simultaneously in each slot.
The consensus rules systematically ignore conflicting signatures, so validators cannot face any penalties unless they publicly admit a malicious intent.
Conflicting votes are resolved using off-chain validator consensus, so the only penalty is solving manual proof-of-work recovery puzzles instead.
questions.explanation: The lesson connects slashing to objective evidence such as double proposals, double attestations, and surround votes. The deterrent does not depend on proving a validator's subjective motive.

questions.question_stem: A report says, "After the Merge, Ethereum stopped using proof-of-work, so all energy used by former Ethereum mining hardware immediately became zero." How would the available reading refine this claim?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum's own protocol energy use dropped because it no longer required PoW mining, but some former mining hardware continued on other chains, so broader ecosystem claims need a clear boundary.
incorrect_answers: The reading's analysis claims that Ethereum secretly retained a proof-of-work layer because it needed fallbacks, but all former mining hardware was deactivated, so protocol energy remained constant.
The reading's data shows that every former GPU miner shut down permanently because of immediate unprofitability, but hardware resale prices rose anyway, so broader ecosystem energy became zero.
The reading's framework treats energy consumption as completely independent of consensus mechanisms because validators use identical hardware, so any environmental claims are irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The available reading supports environmental-boundary reasoning. It distinguishes Ethereum's protocol-level shift away from PoW from the fate of hardware and miners in the wider GPU-mining ecosystem.

questions.question_stem: Why does the available reading use Ethash-equivalent estimates when discussing post-Merge hashrate redistribution?
questions.correct_answer: Different PoW algorithms and GPU performance profiles make raw hashrates misleading, so a common comparison basis is needed.
incorrect_answers: Standardized block intervals and network difficulty rules make raw hashrates identical, so conversion is unnecessary.
Unobserved receiving networks and hardware configurations make direct observation impossible, so a purely theoretical model is used.
Active validator stakes and consensus deposit thresholds make proof-of-work hashrates irrelevant, so a stake metric is favored.
questions.explanation: The reading's methodology point is that raw hashrate numbers across heterogeneous mining algorithms are not directly comparable. Conversion supports a more meaningful estimate of displaced mining capacity.

questions.question_stem: After Ethereum mining revenue disappeared, many GPU miners moved to smaller PoW networks. What outcome does the available reading's incentive logic predict?
questions.correct_answer: Expected reward per unit of computation can fall sharply because many miners compete for smaller reward pools.
incorrect_answers: Individual mining profitability per unit can rise because higher hashrate increases total block rewards.
Protocol difficulty adjustment intervals fail entirely because rapid hashrate migration disables automatic scaling.
Displaced GPU mining rigs validate transactions directly because Ethereum proof-of-stake uses identical hardware.
questions.explanation: The reading connects miner migration to reward-pool size, profitability, and difficulty dynamics. More miners chasing smaller rewards can depress expected returns even if some hardware keeps operating.
